title_en: Don't throw away your old USB charging cables — Repurpose them instead
title_fa: Don't throw away your old USB charging cables — Repurpose them instead
excerpt_en: The charger from your three-generations-ago phone can still be useful. Here are several ways to use old cables, both indoors and out.
excerpt_fa: The charger from your three-generations-ago phone can still be useful. Here are several ways to use old cables, both indoors and out.
content_en:
Don't throw away your old USB charging cables — Repurpose them instead
Turn your junk drawer’s tangled pile of old USB cables into useful everyday tools and crafts.
Most of us have a drawer or box where we keep a tangled pile of old USB cables on top of other cables we probably shouldn't be holding on to. Maybe those charging cables came with a phone you upgraded from three models ago, or maybe they were included with headphones, speakers or a printer you no longer own. Whatever the source, these cables pile up faster than most people realize, especially if you tend to grab newer and faster models every so often.
When decluttering, the instinct may be to throw them straight into the trash, but you should really reconsider. A cable that no longer matches your current devices isn't necessarily useless. Many old USB cables still carry a current perfectly well — they just don't fit the connector on your newest phone or laptop. Others may be worn, frayed or missing a connector altogether, but the copper wiring and durable plastic sheathing still have practical value. Using a frayed cable to conduct a current may pose a fire risk, so be sure you know what you're doing before reusing wiring to power something new. Proceed with extreme caution, or use the cable for one of the current-free uses below.
Rather than defaulting to the trash can or the donation box, there are genuinely creative ways to put those cables back to work. Some ideas require nothing more than a pair of scissors and a few minutes; others call for basic tools like wire cutters and a soldering iron if you're comfortable with electronic projects. Either way, the goal is the same: Get more use out of materials you already own before deciding they're destined for a recycling bin.
How to reuse USB cables that still work
Before cutting into any cable, it's worth testing whether it still conducts power. Such a cable doesn't need to get thrown out. It can keep doing exactly what it was designed for, just in a smaller or more specialized role.
Create a dedicated charging station: Gather up your working cables, bundle them near an outlet close to your desk or kitchen counter and label each one by device type. This keeps cables organized and ensures you're not trying to locate a charger every time a phone or tablet runs low. Even if the cable can't fast-charge your phone, it'll still provide a little bit of power while you're making dinner without having to hunt for a charger in another room.
Put together a dedicated travel charging kit: Those spare cables are just what you need when you go on vacation. If you happen to forget one at the airport or in the hotel room, you won't cry over losing the "good cable." Plus, keeping a separate set packed in a small travel bag means you're never scrambling to gather your tech before a vacation or an unexpected trip.
Reuse cables to power small accessories: Those USB cables you no longer use with your phone and tablet can be just what you need to power LED lights behind your monitor or to illuminate a dark desk corner. If you have basic electronic skills, those old cables with working USB connectors can also power small DIY projects, like simple sensors. You'll probably need a soldering iron and some patience, but you can definitely turn a drawer full of cables into something functional.
How to repurpose USB cables for household and craft projects
Even cables that no longer charge anything reliably still have raw materials worth salvaging. Depending on your imagination and your expertise, there are loads of things you can do with those materials.
The copper core makes surprisingly effective garden twine. Once stripped of its outer shielding and inner insulation, the bare or tinned copper strands are pliable enough to gently tie tomato vines to garden stakes, for instance. In a pinch, the entire cable can even be used to tie a tree to a support stake during a storm.
Indoors, intact cables can be repurposed as plant hangers or picture supports. Cut the connectors from both ends, loop the cable around a pot or a frame and secure it with a knot or hook.
Crafters can have so much fun with such cables. Coiling a flexible cable into a tight spiral and gluing it in place creates a simple coaster. Cable segments threaded through holes drilled into drawers can make unconventional handles if they're secured with a knot or washer. You can even turn these cables, especially ones covered in braided nylon, into keychain lanyards or zipper pulls. If you want to take things a step further, you can make keychains for all family members, leaving the USB connector on the cable. Then, you can find matching female USB ends, arrange them on a tiny plank of some sort, and create a distinctive key mount to put by the door.
For artsy folks, there's also the option of stripping the cables and using those to braid some cool-looking bracelets. You could also arrange them on a canvas or a wood board to create wire art, or make a sculpture out of them by using some armature wire to create the shape, et cetera.
Why you should repurpose and recycle
Even with creative reuse, some cables genuinely reach the end of their usefulness. If that's the case for your cables, you should look into recycling rather than throwing them in the trash. USB cables are made primarily of copper and plastics, materials that don't break down quickly in a landfill. The UN's Global E-waste Monitor 2024 found the world generated 69 million tons of e-waste in 2022, yet only 22.3 percent of it was documented as properly collected and recycled.
Repurposing cables helps keep them out of that waste stream longer and reduces the demand for manufacturing new ones. Big retailers like Best Buy and Staples accept old cables and other small electronics for recycling, often at no cost. If a cable is still in good working order but you simply don't need it, you could also donate it to a local school or nonprofit that runs STEM programs where they could use spare...

title_en: One of the rarest GameCube consoles sells for thousands of dollars today
title_fa: One of the rarest GameCube consoles sells for thousands of dollars today
excerpt_en: While the GameCube came in several colors, a few of the most elusive variations command thousands from game collectors.
excerpt_fa: While the GameCube came in several colors, a few of the most elusive variations command thousands from game collectors.
content_en:
One of the rarest GameCube consoles sells for thousands of dollars today
The most exclusive GameCube variations cost collectors a whole lot of cash.
How much would you be willing to spend when buying a GameCube? While you might be able to find a typical Indigo or Jet Black console for a reasonable price, some of the rarest variations will break the bank and are thus for collectors only.
Sure, there are some attainable relics, like the Pokémon XD: Gale of Darkness and Donkey Konga bundles. Both of those were basic Platinum Silver consoles with custom-branded faceplates featuring Lugia and DK, respectively. The former was available in the US, while the latter was Japan-only.
But speaking of Japanese releases, some of the rarest GameCube models were only released in the country. This includes the Final Fantasy Crystal Chronicles edition, which arrived in a unique color that went beyond the optional cosmetic faceplate. What's more, it sells for thousands of dollars today. For serious collectors, landing one of these units means shelling out a small fortune on the secondary market.
How much is the Crystal Chronicles GameCube worth?
According to eBay sellers and the experts at Consolevariations, the Crystal Chronicles console bundle was limited to 150 units and only available as a prize in a magazine sweepstakes. As an added nod to the well-received RPG, this model was delivered in Crystal White, a cream-like color that sets it apart compared to the more common Pearl White console sold in Europe.
Two of these ultra-rare variants have sold for upwards of $5,000 this year alone, with the most recent sale going for $7,500. Before that, another listing in May sold for just under $7,000. If you're willing to spend top dollar on a piece of Nintendo history, there's currently an unboxed, slightly scuffed listing up for grabs on eBay for $3,750.
It came alongside a Game Boy Player and a copy of Crystal Chronicles. If you're unfamiliar, the Game Boy Player was an add-on that enabled the GameCube to play Game Boy, Game Boy Color and Game Boy Advance cartridges on the TV. In North America, the add-on was only available to buy in Jet Black. Other colors were available throughout Japan, with Crystal White being one of the rarest.
There are other rare GameCube consoles, too
The elusive Heineken GameCube is another standout collector's item; it can be found on eBay for as much as $15,500. In 2002, the Dutch brewer ran a sweepstakes on its website, limiting it to 100 units (50 in Indigo and 50 in Jet Black) for contestants 21 or older.
And while it's not as rare or nearly as expensive secondhand, the Japan-exclusive Gundam Char edition may be the most striking. Like the Final Fantasy variation, this red console and controller were bundled alongside a Game Boy Player.
Tales of Symphonia garnered a similar treatment in 2003 when Nintendo offered the GameCube and Game Boy Player with the title in a mint green bundle. The pastel console was exclusively released in Japan and France with a run of about 10,000 units. This one is more approachable for new collectors; it's much easier to find and goes for no more than $1,500.
According to Consolevariations, some of the rarest unofficial GameCube releases are a pair of airbrushed movie tie-in game consoles originally intended as part of a sweepstakes: one for The Polar Express and the other for The Incredibles. But even with a standard model, your old console could fetch some cash if you no longer use it.

title_en: Apple’s last-gen Mac Mini with the M4 is $150 off
title_fa: Apple’s last-gen Mac Mini with the M4 is $150 off
excerpt_en: Best Buy has a great deal for the rest of the day on the M4 Mac Mini base model that has 16GB RAM and a 256GB SSD. Normally, it doesn’t make a ton of sense to buy the M4 model for its usual $799 price given that the newer, faster M6 version has been available […]
excerpt_fa: Best Buy has a great deal for the rest of the day on the M4 Mac Mini base model that has 16GB RAM and a 256GB SSD. Normally, it doesn’t make a ton of sense to buy the M4 model for its usual $799 price given that the newer, faster M6 version has been available […]
content_en:
Best Buy has a great deal for the rest of the day on the M4 Mac Mini base model that has 16GB RAM and a 256GB SSD. Normally, it doesn’t make a ton of sense to buy the M4 model for its usual $799 price given that the newer, faster M6 version has been available from Amazon for $779.99 (originally $899) for the past couple of weeks. However, at $649 it’s a much more tempting price.
Apple’s last-gen Mac Mini with the M4 is $150 off
At $649, it’s a much better deal. However, the new, faster M6 version is only $130 more.
At $649, it’s a much better deal. However, the new, faster M6 version is only $130 more.
The M4 Mac Mini launched at $599 in 2024, and was an incredible value. Given that this sale price makes it just $50 more than the original price instead of $200, it’s a good time to buy if you want to spend as little as possible on a modern Mac desktop.
Aside from some impressive generational leaps in processing power, you aren’t missing out on a ton by skipping the M6 model and opting for the M4. Their design and ports are nearly identical, and with either model you’ll need to supply your own keyboard, mouse, display, webcam, etc. If you’re on the fence and can’t decide between the M4 and M6 models, I suggest checking out my colleague Antonio’s review of the M6 Mac Mini. The newer model might be well worth the extra $130 cost.
Read our review of the M4 Mac Mini and the M6 Mac Mini
More Verge-approved deals
- Today brought a big discount to LG’s C6 OLEDs lineup, particularly its bigger models. The 55-inch model is $999.99 at Amazon, Best Buy, and Costco (previously $1,399.99), costing a little less than the 42- and 48-inch configurations. The price hasn’t gone below $1,299.99 before, so it’s a good time to consider an upgrade. The 65-inch model is cheaper than before, too. Previously $1,699.99, but normally selling for $1,500 or so, you can grab the larger version for $1,399.99 at Amazon, Best Buy, and Costco. If you have a big room and budget, the 77-inch LG C6H that, like the 48-inch version, has a tandem OLED panel that offers more brightness and better colors, is $1,999.99, down from $2,499.99.
- For $499.99, you can grab a 14-inch HP OmniBook 3 during Best Buy’s deal of the day that has a 2K OLED screen, a capable Snapdragon X ARM processor, 16GB of RAM, and a 256GB SSD. This seems like a fantastic option for anyone on a budget. Its Snapdragon processor can run most x86 Windows 11 apps without much issue, and it’s just a rarity to get these kinds of specs — from the OLED screen to the RAM amount — at $500. My colleague Antonio reviewed the 16-inch version that cuts some corners in the screen department compared to this 14-inch model.
- It’s time to get spooky if you haven’t already planned your run of games for Halloween. The spectacular Silent Hill 2 remake is down to $21.34 on Steam for PC via Fanatical, a third-party site I’ve shopped from numerous times. If you’re alright with spending more, Resident Evil Requiem is one of Capcom’s several great 2026 games, and it’s $20 off at Amazon on all platforms, costing $49.99.

content_en:
Today, I’m talking with Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, who has a lot of thoughts about AI, tech, and privacy.
JB Pritzker thinks AI could help us live to 100 — or threaten us like nukes
The Illinois governor on AI, data centers, privacy, and Trump.
If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
If you’ve been listening to the show, you know that one of my running theories is that those issues are driving a big and maybe kind of unexpected political realignment — and with the midterms coming up next month, and early voting already underway in a lot of places, the stakes are pretty high right now.
So I asked Gov. Pritzker about all that, and he was surprisingly willing to dive right into the absolute existential weeds of what government is even for. You’ll hear him say — and it’s hard to disagree — that some problems are just collective action problems that require the government to do a lot of work. We can’t solve all these problems one at a time, or even one state at a time. It’s a pretty deep conversation, and we really got into it on a lot of issues.
And of course, I had to ask him: Are the Bears gonna stay in Illinois?
Before we get going, do me a favor and subscribe to Decoder on YouTube, where we put out new episodes every Monday and Thursday.
Okay: Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker. Here we go.
Gov. JB Pritzker, you’re the governor of Illinois. Welcome to Decoder.
Thanks, Nilay. Great to be with you.
I am very excited to talk to you. We’re in the heart of midterm season. You are running for reelection. I have to tell you. I have to be very honest with you. I personally feel a lot of pressure in this interview, not only because I’m speaking to a governor, but because I went to school in Chicago. My sister still lives in Chicago. My wife grew up in Illinois. Her entire family is farmers in North Central Illinois. Boy, do I have a list of questions for you. I have to do a good job here.
Well, we’re claiming you. Now that I know all that, we’re claiming you. You’re an Illinoisan.
Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here.
I don’t know about that. I grew up in Wisconsin. Here’s my first question for you. I’m a die-hard Packers fan. Are you going to let the Bears move to Indiana?
That is not our intention. We are, in fact, in discussions with the Bears and the NFL about keeping the Bears either in Chicago or in Arlington Heights, but in Illinois.
I’m saying, as a Packers fan, nothing is funnier than the outcome of the Bears moving to Indiana. I just want to put that out there. Openly biased in this case — I own two shares of that stock — but I’m going to make the comparison here. And the reason I started there is not only because I think that’s a funny outcome, although I do, but it feels like we are in the middle of a generational political realignment.
I’m sure you feel that, in this election campaign, the idea of big business and how that should interact with the government, and how the government should be able to push back on big business and not give in to big business. All of that feels up for grabs.
And the comparison I will make in this specific case is your fellow governor, Gavin Newsom, in California. They sued the Ellison family, Paramount, over the Warner Brothers merger. Paramount threatened to leave. They made a lot of noise about Nashville, Texas, Miami, or wherever you make noise about these days, and it feels like Newsom caved. It feels like he pressured his Attorney General, Rob Bonta, to settle that lawsuit and keep them there.
They settled the lawsuit. The next day, the Ellison family is like, “We never... We’re from California. We would never leave.” I see a parallel here with the Bears that is connected to that larger realignment, how government and business should interact. Do you see that parallel? Do you feel that realignment?
Well, what I can tell you is we’re pretty tough negotiators in Chicago and Illinois, and that’s really what we’re in the midst of now with the Bears. But I understand your point about realignment. I mean, there is a generational change, and I think it’s also an attitudinal change about protecting taxpayers, protecting people who frankly are among the most vulnerable to all the technology that’s overtaking people’s lives and invading people’s homes.
And so I do believe that the government has to be more active now and become a fighter for our people and not just a collaborator with business on everything. I’m a businessman, as you know, before I became governor. But I also know that, for the people of Illinois anyway, my job is to protect the working people of this state who often don’t have anybody protecting them except a government that will stand up for them. So that’s kind of the realignment that I see.
And that generational shift, I agree with you. It’s partly a Democratic Party generational shift. Generationally, we’re a little more aggressive. And I’m probably older than the next generation that’s already possibly taking office this November. I’m 61 years old, but I think of myself as having come out of the tech world and as somebody who has been a fighter for progressive values that, yeah, we’ve got to become more aggressive and make sure we’re standing up for our people.
There are two places where I see the realignment in particular. One is data centers, one is privacy, and you just see that as a bipartisan backlash to those things. I would actually add a third, which is antitrust broadly. It’s weird if you go into Silicon Valley. David Sacks is retweeting Lina Khan from the Biden administration talking about whether the AI industry needs an antitrust exemption to manage safety.
They both agree that these companies don’t need antitrust exemptions. They actually should be more competitive. Again, putting that in the context of regulating these companies, thinking about the dynamic...

title_en: What the orange light on your PlayStation 5 is actually telling you
title_fa: What the orange light on your PlayStation 5 is actually telling you
excerpt_en: The PS5 shows a variety of light colors to indicate its status, and orange thankfully isn't the alert you might expect from that color.
excerpt_fa: The PS5 shows a variety of light colors to indicate its status, and orange thankfully isn't the alert you might expect from that color.
content_en:
What the orange light on your PlayStation 5 is actually telling you
Unlike many orange icons and lights, this one isn't a warning sign.
Orange isn't the most reassuring color to see displayed on a device. It's something that can trigger a visceral reaction of panic, given its use for elements like check engine lights in a car and faulty power supplies for past consoles. Thankfully, on a PlayStation 5 it's nothing to worry about; it just means the console has entered Rest Mode. An unrelated orange light on your PS5 controller below the PS button indicates that your mic is muted — press that button to unmute.
Rest Mode is an incredibly handy feature that saves power while still allowing your console to perform basic tasks. Depending on your PS5's settings, it can work to charge your controllers and download games while consuming only a few watts. Entering Rest Mode after a set period of inactivity is part of the console's factory settings, but you can easily adjust this or disable it entirely.
To enter Rest Mode when you're done playing, simply press the power button on the front of the console for a moment. Alternatively, hit the PS button on your controller to open the control center, then go to Power > Enter Rest Mode. Never unplug your PS5 when you see the orange light, as it's not fully powered off in that state. Select Turn Off PS5 from the Power menu and wait for the system lights to go out before unplugging it.
How to change your PlayStation 5's Rest Mode settings
If your PS5 is entering Rest Mode from inactivity faster than you want, you can change the timer for this in its settings:
-
From the home screen, select Settings at the top-right.
-
Select System, then Power Saving.
-
Select Set Time Until PS5 Enters Rest Mode.
From here, you can set how long the console will remain inactive before entering Rest Mode, with separate settings for media playback and while playing games. If you'd like, you can also choose to have your PS5 never enter Rest Mode, even after prolonged inactivity.
Also in the Power Saving section of system settings, select Features Available in Rest Mode to determine how much your PS5 will do while resting. This is where you can choose to power the USB ports, update games, upload saves to the cloud or play games remotely using a PlayStation Portal or other device via remote play.
PlayStation 5 hardware warning signs
While an orange light on your PS5 is nothing to worry about, there are other signs when your console is having trouble and might need repair. The console has been around for nearly six years, and there's no clear timeline for how long a PS5 should be expected to last. Sony's track record of continuing to support the PS4 with updates bodes well for the firmware side as the PS5 gets on in years, but it's smart to keep an eye on your hardware. Considering how the PS5 has gone up in price since release, the earlier you can address and fix problems (and in turn avoid having to purchase a new console), the better.
One of the most common PS5 issues is overheating, which can either be a product of the environment it's in (like blocked or dusty exhaust vents) or the cooling system naturally degrading over time. Possible signs of overheating include the console shutting down unexpectedly, extremely hot or loud air flow coming from its vents or even an on-screen warning about the console's temperature. If it continues to be a problem even after you've cleaned out dust and placed it in a well-ventilated area, it might be worth bringing it to a professional to have the thermal paste replaced. Repeated overheating can damage internal components and lead to more problems later on.
Another one of the most frequent PS5 problems is GPU failure, which presents as visual glitches like screen flickering, static or multicolored lines. These can also be caused by HDMI issues, however, so it's worth trying another high-quality HDMI cable and HDMI port on your TV before assuming your GPU is failing. Plugging your PS5 into another monitor or TV is also a good step to rule out the display as the root cause.
If problems persist, it's likely that your GPU is failing. Unfortunately, because of the specific parts a PS5 uses, the solution for this is to either send the console to Sony for repair or take it to a specialized repair shop.

title_en: Don't throw away your old graphics card — here's what you can do with it
title_fa: Don't throw away your old graphics card — here's what you can do with it
excerpt_en: An old GPU has lots of potential for a second life, from adding more horsepower to your current machine to crafting a purpose-built second one.
excerpt_fa: An old GPU has lots of potential for a second life, from adding more horsepower to your current machine to crafting a purpose-built second one.
content_en:
Don't throw away your old graphics card — here's what you can do with it
Some older graphics cards are still worth almost as much as they initially cost, so don’t waste their potential.
Especially in the current climate, you probably don't have to be told that throwing away your old graphics card is a bad idea. They're expensive, and you can repurpose your prior one after you upgrade. Every three to five years is a common cadence for GPU upgrades, so it's important to think about what happens to your investment when the next cycle comes around.
The most popular card in the latest Steam hardware survey is the Nvidia GeForce RTX 5070, which is installed in 6.15 percent of surveyed systems. It launched at $549 and can now cost more than $800 because of memory and silicon price inflation. Increased prices mean more people will use their GPUs for longer, which may stretch the typical upgrade cycle.
Just because you've outgrown your graphics card doesn't mean everyone else has, so selling your old GPU to get some value back is a good option. An eBay search at the time of writing shows some used RTX 3060s selling for almost as much as they originally cost. Even the 10-year-old $249 GTX 1060 is typically listed at $50 to $100 in good condition, though these are always subject to fluctuation.
What to do with an old graphics card
You can repurpose your old graphics card by installing it into your home media server to handle hardware-accelerated video encoding and decoding using Nvidia's NVENC or AMD's AMF. Both Jellyfin and Plex support hardware-accelerated streaming, so your old GPU can gain new life converting video codecs in real time to offload tasks from the processor.
Alternatively, you can build a PC to connect to your TV that also runs as a gaming console. You don't need state-of-the-art performance for light indie games or emulation, and sometimes older hardware can work better with past releases designed for older standards. Use it to run titles built using legacy code libraries, DirectX 9-era games, or to gain extra HDMI/DisplayPort connections to drive additional displays.
Using the card in a spare slot in your main PC to run legacy software may also work, if you have enough power and ventilation. However, there are caveats to running two GPUs in one chassis. You'll need a power supply and motherboard capable of handling dual GPUs and may bump into PCIe lane limits. If your processor uses lane splitting, a second card can degrade the performance of your primary GPU, which is a problem. Check your motherboard manual to see how it handles different expansion slots before you commit resources to this project.
Even more: streaming, gaming, encoding and AI
Gamers have even more options to repurpose an old GPU. Try running Lossless Scaling ($6.99 on Steam) on your old card as second-fiddle support for your new one, or use it to capture in-game video while the primary GPU runs the game. You might build a separate PC for capturing video streams, or as a video encoding and editing rig handling tasks in DaVinci Resolve or Blender. It can even be a good option for running local AI workloads, given how heavily those rely on VRAM.
Holding onto the video card to have a spare in case one fails isn't a bad idea if you have no other use in mind. Just be aware the money you could make selling it will drop over time, and remember to store it safely in an antistatic bag.
Finally, a word about recycling: even if you plan to get rid of it, you shouldn't throw electronics out with the trash. Companies that do e-waste recycling will take your old card to break it down. Even if your old card is irreparable, the gold, copper and aluminum it contains will have value somewhere, so recycling it is way better than chucking electronics into a landfill.

title_en: Apple updates guidelines to ban nudify apps masquerading as regular apps to pass review
title_fa: Apple updates guidelines to ban nudify apps masquerading as regular apps to pass review
excerpt_en: The company updated its guidelines with strong language around AI and user-generated content, and how app developers should include enough preventative measures to moderate objectionable or offensive content.
excerpt_fa: The company updated its guidelines with strong language around AI and user-generated content, and how app developers should include enough preventative measures to moderate objectionable or offensive content.
content_en:
Apple tightened its developer guidelines over the weekend to ban apps that use AI to create offensive content, as well as those that masquerade as regular apps to pass the App Store review process and then turn into nudify apps, or surface those features prominently.
The company updated its guidelines with strong language around AI and user-generated content, and how app developers should include enough preventative measures to moderate objectionable or offensive content.
“Apps that host user-generated content are required to filter objectionable material, give users a way to report offensive content, and let users block abusive accounts. Apps containing hidden or undocumented features are also prohibited on the App Store, including apps that misrepresent their purpose during review and only reveal harmful capabilities — such as ‘nudification’ — after approval, a tactic commonly known as bait-and-switch,” the company said in a blog post.
Apple said that it will remove apps that add features not present in the version submitted for App Store review.
The iPhone maker has also updated the language in its legal section to reinforce that it will bar apps promoting human trafficking and exploitation of children.
Apple said last year its review process blocked over 150,000 apps from reaching users and removed 193,000 developer accounts due to fraud and abuse.
In July, the city of San Francisco ordered both Apple and Google to clean up and delete nudification apps from their app stores. City Attorney David Chiu accused the companies of profiting from these apps through store fees. And in April, a Tech Transparency Project report indicated that both tech giants’ stores hosted multiple nudify apps, some of which were rated as suitable for minors.

The iPhone maker has also updated the language in its legal section to reinforce that it will bar apps promoting human trafficking and exploitation of children.
Apple said last year its review process blocked over 150,000 apps from reaching users and removed 193,000 developer accounts due to fraud and abuse.
In July, the city of San Francisco ordered both Apple and Google to clean up and delete nudification apps from their app stores. City Attorney David Chiu accused the companies of profiting from these apps through store fees. And in April, a Tech Transparency Project report indicated that both tech giants’ stores hosted multiple nudify apps, some of which were rated as suitable for minors.

title_en: 6 unexpected uses for your old PlayStation 3
title_fa: 6 unexpected uses for your old PlayStation 3
excerpt_en: The PlayStation 3 arrived in 2006 and shouldn't have any right finding a place in a modern media center. Here's a number of reasons why it should make a return.
excerpt_fa: The PlayStation 3 arrived in 2006 and shouldn't have any right finding a place in a modern media center. Here's a number of reasons why it should make a return.
content_en:
6 unexpected uses for your old PlayStation 3
Don't let it gather dust just yet.
Two decades, 87 million units and two new generations later, the PlayStation 3 is well into its end-of-life phase. As expected, most third-party services have dropped support for the console, with Crunchyroll pulling its app in 2022, followed by Plex in 2023, then Netflix in March 2026.
But that doesn't make this fine piece of hardware useless. In fact, to this day, the old PlayStation 3 still has some surprise tricks and unexpected uses up its thick plastic sleeves, so there's no reason to let it gather dust.
With the right steps and a few hours, you can use your old PlayStation 3 to stream movies from your PC, play Blu-ray discs, rip CDs and emulate your favorite retro games. If none of those do the trick, maybe something beneath the old PlayStation 3's plastic body will.
Use your old PlayStation 3 as a disc player
The disc player on the PlayStation 3 doesn't only play games; it also plays audio CDs, DVDs and Blu-rays right out of the box. You don't need to go to any secret menu or install custom firmware, simply slot in the disc and enjoy. To make things even better, the PlayStation 3 has a built-in upscaler that can enhance standard-definition DVDs to HD (up to 1080p) when connected via its HDMI cable. In other words, your old media can look sharper and cleaner.
To turn on upscaling: From the main menu, go to Settings > Video Settings then scroll down to BD/DVD Upscaler and press X. Choose your preferred option from Normal, Double Scale, Full Screen and Off (disables upscaling).
If you want the full media experience, you can ditch the DualShock 3 controller for the PS3's BD Remote control which gives you complete command over playback. Do note that you'll need to keep your PS3 updated if you want to continue watching Blu-ray films on it. This is due to the Advanced Access Content System (AACS) copyright-protection technology. Fortunately, Sony still issues this update about once a year. If your console is offline, you can download the update from Sony onto a USB drive then install it from there.
Stream your PC's media library
That old PlayStation 3 supports Digital Living Network Alliance (DLNA), a home networking standard that allows you to stream content from another device on the same network. The simplest example would be from PC to your PS3. Using this, you can watch locally-stored movies, home videos and music from your PC directly on your TV. Setting it up is also pretty straightforward.
To enable it on your PS3, go to Settings > Network Settings and enable Media Server Connection. Shared libraries should now appear under the Photo, Music and Video columns in the main menu. On a Windows PC, you can use the built-in Windows Media Player, but it limits the experience to only playing file formats the PS3 supports (which is not a lot). The free Universal Media Server solves this by converting unsupported files in real time, and it runs on Windows, MacOS and Linux.
If you want a simpler solution, you can fill up a USB flash drive with your favorite movies and TV shows, then simply plug it into your PlayStation 3. You'll need to format the USB drive to FAT32 first, then create specific root folders named VIDEO, MUSIC and PICTURES so your console can read the files. FAT32 caps individual files at 4GB and video quality is limited to 1080p, so keep that in mind before you copy over your media.
Play your favorite retro games
Another good use for your old PlayStation 3 is retro gaming. Every PS3 model is backward compatible with PS1 games, but unfortunately not every model runs PS2 discs. Only the early 'fat' consoles can play second-generation titles. If your PS3 isn't one of the chosen few, you'll have to rely on the official Digital PS2 Classics on the PlayStation 3 store. Surprisingly, the PlayStation Store is still available on the PS3, but it no longer accepts credit cards or PayPal, so you'll need a PlayStation gift card.
If you're willing to take it a step further, you can get your PS3 to run emulators for other retro consoles including the Super Nintendo and Sega CD. But to do that you'll need to jailbreak your old PlayStation 3, and that requires a bit of technical know-how. Be aware that this violates Sony's licensing terms, and can brick the console.
Rip your CD collection
The PlayStation 3 can easily turn your collection of CDs into a digital music library; no PC, secret menu or custom software needed. Simply insert a disc, then go to Music on the main menu, highlight the CD icon, press the triangle button and select Import. The ripped tracks save to the console's hard drive, and from there you can sort them into playlists and easily play them right on the console whenever you like. Do note that some copy-protected CDs aren't supported and all formats are lossy, so you won't get a perfect copy of your collection.
By default, the tracks are saved as 128 kbps AAC files which is just fine for casual listening. Luckily, you can raise the quality by going to: Settings > Music Settings > Audio CD Import. Choose MP3 320 Kbps or AAC for the best sound quality. On supported PS3 games, you can play stored music in the background while gaming.
As an added bonus, you can transfer those ripped tracks to a USB drive. Simply plug in your storage (make sure it's been formatted to FAT32), find the track or album under the Music menu, then press the triangle button, select Copy and choose your USB drive as the destination.

There's always somebody willing to pay cash for your old PlayStation 3 that's been gathering dust in a cupboard for years. Finding a buyer can be easier than you think, especially when you know where to look.

title_en: Musk pledges to give ‘every kid in America’ one of his SpaceX shares
title_fa: Musk pledges to give ‘every kid in America’ one of his SpaceX shares
excerpt_en: Musk's post came just a few hours after Anthropic promised to put 5% of its shares into a new "public benefit fund," which it intends to use to make "large donations to traditional nonprofits or direct distributions to specific populations" after its upcoming IPO.
excerpt_fa: Musk's post came just a few hours after Anthropic promised to put 5% of its shares into a new "public benefit fund," which it intends to use to make "large donations to traditional nonprofits or direct distributions to specific populations" after its upcoming IPO.
content_en:
Elon Musk claims he will give one of his SpaceX shares to “every kid in America” in 2027, which would result in a gift worth more than $10 billion based on the current $146 share price of his combination spaceflight and AI company. That’s roughly 1% of his $1 trillion net worth.
It’s not clear how Musk plans to do this, though he said in a separate post that he wants to give the shares “directly to the public,” and that this will be the “first of many” shares he’ll donate.
President Donald Trump, who Musk spent around $300 million to help elect, has set up bank accounts for children through the Treasury, called Trump Accounts, that can accept stock donations from wealthy donors.
Musk did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Musk’s post came just a few hours after Anthropic promised to put 5% of its shares into a new “public benefit fund,” which it intends to use to make “large donations to traditional nonprofits or direct distributions to specific populations” after its upcoming IPO.
On Sunday afternoon, Musk replied directly to Anthropic’s post on X about its new fund, suggesting the company should give “directly to the public” instead.
“This is what I will be doing,” he wrote in another reply four hours later. Then, overnight, he announced his plans to donate SpaceX stock.
There are currently more than 70 million children under the age of 18 in the United States, according to the Federal Interagency Forum on Child and Family Statistics. Musk owns around 849 million Class A common shares of SpaceX and more than 5.5 billion Class B supervoting shares. He stands to earn many more.
Musk’s philanthropic giving to date has been almost exclusively done through his Musk Foundation. Despite his negative opinions about philanthropy, it’s the fifth-largest private charitable foundation in the U.S. However, a recent review by The Economist showed that a majority of the total money laid out by the Musk Foundation over the years has gone to entities tied to Musk in some way. Nearly 60% has gone to another charity, called The Foundation, run by his money manager, Jared Birchall.

title_en: Khosla Ventures doubles down on Even Healthcare to challenge India’s hospital economics
title_fa: Khosla Ventures doubles down on Even Healthcare to challenge India’s hospital economics
excerpt_en: Even Healthcare reaches a $300 million valuation in a Khosla Ventures-led round as it plans to expand its hospital network in India.
excerpt_fa: Even Healthcare reaches a $300 million valuation in a Khosla Ventures-led round as it plans to expand its hospital network in India.
content_en:
Even Healthcare has raised $50 million in a funding round led by Khosla Ventures, as the Indian startup seeks to change how hospitals in the world’s most populous country make money and how doctors are rewarded.
The all-equity Series B round also saw participation from Alpha Wave and valued it at $300 million, triple its valuation 18 months ago, according to Even. The latest funding brings Even’s total capital raised to more than $120 million.
Hospitals in India typically earn more when patients undergo additional tests, procedures, or longer stays, even when they may not need them. Even wants to change that by focusing on patient care rather than pushing unnecessary treatments that drive up medical bills.
That approach has continued to appeal to Khosla Ventures, which has invested in Even since its seed round in 2021. The Silicon Valley venture firm is doubling down as Even moves to build and operate hospitals of its own, giving it greater control over patient care and costs.
Vinod Khosla, founder of Khosla Ventures, said Even’s approach goes beyond fixing individual parts of a fragmented healthcare system by bringing financing, technology, and care delivery together. The goal, he said in a prepared statement, is to reward better health outcomes rather than greater use of healthcare services.
“The clinical and economic results so far give us conviction that this can become an important new model for healthcare in India and beyond,” Khosla said.
Initially, Even relied on partner hospitals to treat its members, but co-founder Mayank Banerjee said in an interview that the startup began questioning that model after finding that patients had undergone tests or been recommended surgeries it considered unnecessary.
“We think patients are getting not only a bad experience, but insurers are getting a bad economic deal. And as a result, we decided to fix it by building our own hospitals,” Banerjee told TechCrunch.
Even has since opened two hospitals in Bengaluru, both of which reached operational profitability, excluding depreciation, within a year of opening, Banerjee stated. The startup plans to open five more hospitals in the southern Indian city over the next six months, funded by its latest round.
Banerjee told TechCrunch that Even leases hospital buildings on 20-year agreements and spends on fitting them out and buying medical equipment.
Unlike hospitals where doctors may have financial incentives to recommend more procedures, Even pays its doctors fixed salaries — not tying their compensation to the number of tests or surgeries they perform, though Banerjee said doctors can earn bonuses based on patient-reported clinical outcomes.
The same principle extends to hospital management, whose compensation is not linked to the number of procedures performed, Banerjee told TechCrunch. Managers, he said, receive salaries and company-wide incentives, while marketing teams focus on bringing in patients instead of the revenue those patients generate. Moreover, every employee, including doctors and other hospital staff, receives equity in Even. The idea is to give employees a stake in the startup’s long-term performance, not to reward them for generating more medical bills.
Most of Even’s revenue comes from patients paying for treatment, Banerjee said. The startup also generates revenue through its relationships with insurers. It is also working with insurer partners on a model that could compensate it for hospitalizations it helps prevent, not simply for providing more treatment.
Banerjee told TechCrunch that Even tracks how patients recover after treatment using established medical scoring systems. In the case of knee replacements, for instance, it uses the Oxford Knee Score to measure pain and mobility. The startup publishes results on its website, alongside figures from other healthcare systems for comparison.
Even says its hospitals have an unplanned readmission rate of less than 1%, compared with an industry benchmark of 8% to 15%. Furthermore, it claims patients spend 40% less time in the hospital and that its approach has saved insurers more than ₹500 million (about $5.27 million).
Jai Sajnani, a partner at Khosla Ventures, told TechCrunch that the early performance of Even’s hospitals was a key reason the firm led the round. “We look forward to helping the Even team put quality care within reach of every family in Bengaluru and across India,” he said.
Even is still losing money, though. The startup posted a net loss of ₹902 million (about $9.50 million) in fiscal 2025, nearly 25% more than the previous year, on revenue of ₹272 million (about $2.86 million), regulatory filings show.
In August, Even also laid off about 350 employees, according to Indian startup-news website Entrackr. Banerjee acknowledged the restructuring and called it a difficult decision. He said the affected employees received severance, extended health insurance, and accelerated equity vesting.
Even currently employs about 650 people, including around 300 doctors full-time. The startup has about 250,000 members and has recorded more than 750,000 patient interactions since its launch in 2021, including consultations, diagnostic tests, and surgeries, Banerjee said.
Banerjee told TechCrunch that Even could turn profitable within months if it stopped spending on expansion, but the startup is choosing to grow instead. He declined to say when the startup expects to become profitable.
“Right now, we’re investing in growth and serving more patients,” Banerjee said.

title_en: What do all the lights on your Netgear router mean, and which ones actually matter?
title_fa: What do all the lights on your Netgear router mean, and which ones actually matter?
excerpt_en: Some router symbols are obvious, while others take a bit of work to decipher. Their lights can vary, too.
excerpt_fa: Some router symbols are obvious, while others take a bit of work to decipher. Their lights can vary, too.
content_en:
What do all the lights on your Netgear router mean, and which ones actually matter?
Depending on their colors, most of those flashing lights are a good sign.
The front of a Netgear router, like many routers, is dotted with a wide array of lights and symbols. Though some of the symbols like the power indicator are straightforward, the lights themselves can be much less clear. They often vary in color; sometimes they're blinking and other times they're solid. If you've never picked up the manual, deciphering what each of the many lights means doesn't come naturally.
Understanding what each of the indicators on your Netgear router signify is important for troubleshooting, as well as making sure everything is running as it should. Although some lights are usually more important than others, they all serve a purpose. Whether you have a standard router or one of the company's mesh Wi-Fi systems, this is how to better understand what your Netgear device is telling you.
The most important lights on your Netgear router
These are the lights on a router that are generally the most important to pay attention to, as they're indicators of the most impactful stats like power and overall internet connection status.
The power LED
Represented by the typical power symbol, this indicates information about your device's firmware, as well as its power status. Unsurprisingly, this will be off if your router has no power.
- Solid green or white: The router is on and ready.
- Solid amber: The router is turning on.
- Blinking amber: The router's firmware is upgrading, or you pressed the reset button.
- Blinking white: The router's firmware is corrupted.
- Blinking white and amber: The router is in access point mode, which means it's acting as a connection point for other devices instead of handling its normal router functions. Some features like VPN and remote management will be unavailable.
If your router isn't working properly, restart it first. In case it's fully unresponsive, you may need to do a factory reset.
Internet LED
The icon and light with a small circle orbiting a larger one shows your general connection status:
- Off: The router is not connected to a modem; check the Ethernet cable to make sure it's fully inserted and not damaged.
- Solid green or white: The internet connection is ready.
- Solid amber: An Ethernet cable connection to the modem has been detected.
- Blinking white: The port is sending and/or receiving traffic.
Wi-Fi LED
Represented by a small dot with two curves on each side, this light shows general Wi-Fi traffic.
- Off: The router's Wi-Fi radios are off.
- Solid white: The router's Wi-Fi radios are operating.
- Blinking white: The router is sending and/or receiving Wi-Fi traffic.
Other lights on your Netgear router
Further lights on your Netgear router are more useful for specific troubleshooting, or if you're plugging additional devices into the router.
Wi-Fi band LEDS
Every modern router should have lights for the 2.4GHz and 5GHz bands, as these have long been the standard. For a Wi-Fi 6E model or newer, you'll also see a 6GHz light for that modern band. The lights will differ depending on the bands currently in use, but the lights have the same meanings for each band.
- Off: This particular Wi-Fi radio is off.
- Solid white: The Wi-Fi radio in question is operating.
- Blinking white: The router is sending and/or receiving traffic over the corresponding Wi-Fi radio.
USB LEDs
Your router will have one of these lights for each USB port it includes, represented by the trident USB symbol or the text "USB 3.0."
- Off: No USB device is connected to the port, or the Safely Remove Hardware button was pressed and you're clear to remove the attached device.
- Blinking: A USB device is trying to connect.
- Solid green or white: A USB device is connected and ready to use.
Ethernet LEDs
These are labeled by numbers, with each representing an Ethernet port on the router. The color represents the speed of the connection: white or green for 1 Gbps connections, and amber for slower 100 Mbps or 10 Mbps Ethernet.
- Off: Nothing is connected to the port.
- Solid: A powered-on device is connected to the port.
- Blinking: The port is sending and/or receiving traffic.
WPS LED
Represented by what looks like a router with signals coming out of it, this light indicates the success of a WPS (Wi-Fi Protected Setup) connection, which allows you to add devices to your network without entering the network name and password. For the best router security, you should disable this.
- Off: No WPS connection.
- Blinking: A WPS connection is in progress.
- Solid: The WPS connection was successful.
Reading the lights on a Netgear Orbi mesh system
The lights on Netgear's Orbi Wi-Fi mesh system are minimalist compared to a typical router's, and represent key statuses slightly differently. There's a light in the bottom-front of the device, plus one at the back. The light in the front represents the connection status, while the one at the back is tied to the device's power and firmware.
The front LED lights
- Solid blue light: The connection between the router and satellite is strong.
- Solid amber light: The connection between the router and satellite is OK, but not great.
- Solid magenta light: There's no backhaul connection or no internet connection.
- No light: The Orbi is not receiving power.
The back LED light
- Solid green light: The router and satellite are powered on.
- Solid amber light: The device is rebooting.
- Pulsing amber light: The device is updating its firmware or resetting to factory settings.
- Pulsing red light: Possible hardware issues or connectivity failure.
- No light: The Orbi is not receiving power.
content_fa:
What do all the lights on your Netgear router mean, and which ones actually matter?
Depending on their colors, most of those flashing lights are a good sign.
The front of a Netgear router, like many routers, is dotted with a wide array of lights and symbols. Though some of the symbols like the power indicator are straightforward, the lights themselves can be much less clear. They often vary in color; sometimes they're blinking and other times they're solid. If you've never picked up the manual, deciphering what each of the many lights means doesn't come naturally.
Understanding what each of the indicators on your Netgear router signify is important for troubleshooting, as well as making sure everything is running as it should. Although some lights are usually more important than others, they all serve a purpose. Whether you have a standard router or one of the company's mesh Wi-Fi systems, this is how to better understand what your Netgear device is telling you.
The most important lights on your Netgear router
These are the lights on a router that are generally the most important to pay attention to, as they're indicators of the most impactful stats like power and overall internet connection status.
The power LED
Represented by the typical power symbol, this indicates information about your device's firmware, as well as its power status. Unsurprisingly, this will be off if your router has no power.
- Solid green or white: The router is on and ready.
- Solid amber: The router is turning on.
- Blinking amber: The router's firmware is upgrading, or you pressed the reset button.
- Blinking white: The router's firmware is corrupted.
- Blinking white and amber: The router is in access point mode, which means it's acting as a connection point for other devices instead of handling its normal router functions. Some features like VPN and remote management will be unavailable.
If your router isn't working properly, restart it first. In case it's fully unresponsive, you may need to do a factory reset.
Internet LED
The icon and light with a small circle orbiting a larger one shows your general connection status:
- Off: The router is not connected to a modem; check the Ethernet cable to make sure it's fully inserted and not damaged.
- Solid green or white: The internet connection is ready.
- Solid amber: An Ethernet cable connection to the modem has been detected.
- Blinking white: The port is sending and/or receiving traffic.
Wi-Fi LED
Represented by a small dot with two curves on each side, this light shows general Wi-Fi traffic.
- Off: The router's Wi-Fi radios are off.
- Solid white: The router's Wi-Fi radios are operating.
- Blinking white: The router is sending and/or receiving Wi-Fi traffic.
Other lights on your Netgear router
Further lights on your Netgear router are more useful for specific troubleshooting, or if you're plugging additional devices into the router.
Wi-Fi band LEDS
Every modern router should have lights for the 2.4GHz and 5GHz bands, as these have long been the standard. For a Wi-Fi 6E model or newer, you'll also see a 6GHz light for that modern band. The lights will differ depending on the bands currently in use, but the lights have the same meanings for each band.
- Off: This particular Wi-Fi radio is off.
- Solid white: The Wi-Fi radio in question is operating.
- Blinking white: The router is sending and/or receiving traffic over the corresponding Wi-Fi radio.
USB LEDs
Your router will have one of these lights for each USB port it includes, represented by the trident USB symbol or the text "USB 3.0."
- Off: No USB device is connected to the port, or the Safely Remove Hardware button was pressed and you're clear to remove the attached device.
- Blinking: A USB device is trying to connect.
- Solid green or white: A USB device is connected and ready to use.
Ethernet LEDs
These are labeled by numbers, with each representing an Ethernet port on the router. The color represents the speed of the connection: white or green for 1 Gbps connections, and amber for slower 100 Mbps or 10 Mbps Ethernet.
- Off: Nothing is connected to the port.
- Solid: A powered-on device is connected to the port.
- Blinking: The port is sending and/or receiving traffic.
WPS LED
Represented by what looks like a router with signals coming out of it, this light indicates the success of a WPS (Wi-Fi Protected Setup) connection, which allows you to add devices to your network without entering the network name and password. For the best router security, you should disable this.
- Off: No WPS connection.
- Blinking: A WPS connection is in progress.
- Solid: The WPS connection was successful.
Reading the lights on a Netgear Orbi mesh system
The lights on Netgear's Orbi Wi-Fi mesh system are minimalist compared to a typical router's, and represent key statuses slightly differently. There's a light in the bottom-front of the device, plus one at the back. The light in the front represents the connection status, while the one at the back is tied to the device's power and firmware.
The front LED lights
- Solid blue light: The connection between the router and satellite is strong.
- Solid amber light: The connection between the router and satellite is OK, but not great.
- Solid magenta light: There's no backhaul connection or no internet connection.
- No light: The Orbi is not receiving power.
The back LED light
- Solid green light: The router and satellite are powered on.
- Solid amber light: The device is rebooting.
- Pulsing amber light: The device is updating its firmware or resetting to factory settings.
- Pulsing red light: Possible hardware issues or connectivity failure.
- No light: The Orbi is not receiving power.

title_en: What does the orange dot on your Samsung Galaxy Watch mean?
title_fa: What does the orange dot on your Samsung Galaxy Watch mean?
excerpt_en: You might sometimes see an orange dot on the left side of your Galaxy Watch's screen. Here's what is tells you.
excerpt_fa: You might sometimes see an orange dot on the left side of your Galaxy Watch's screen. Here's what is tells you.
content_en:
What does the orange dot on your Samsung Galaxy Watch mean?
We have the answer.
Whether you're getting into digital watches for the first time, or transitioning to Galaxy watches from another brand (such as from the Apple Watch Ultra 4 to the Galaxy Watch Ultra 2), Samsung's wrist-worn tech has its fair share of unique attributes. One such feature is the little orange dot that appears to the far left of your watch screen. While it might be a strange quirk if you're not used to it, it's pretty simple to explain.
Throughout the history of the Galaxy Watch, one little orange dot has been a constant. In fact, the dot is present on the latest watch models (including both the Galaxy Watch 8 and the Galaxy Watch 9, as well as the Ultra 2). This little dot is a minimalist way for the Galaxy Watch to display some important information.
The meaning of the Samsung Galaxy Watch's orange dot
The orange dot on Galaxy Watches is a notification indicator — specifically for unread notifications. This dot will remain on your watch's face until you've read all of those outstanding notifications, at which point it will then scurry off. If the dot on your screen is red instead of orange, that means you have an urgent message that you ought to check as soon as possible.
An orange dot is nonetheless common and harmless, but it can be toggled off if it doesn't suit your fancy. Simply head to Settings > Notifications > Advanced Settings and toggle off New notification indicator on watch face. You can also turn the indicator off via a Samsung phone linked to your watch, where you'll simply need to go to the Wearable app and head Watch Settings > Notifications > Advanced notification settings and toggle off New notification indicator on watch face.
Other symbols on the Galaxy Watch
This dot isn't the only symbol of its kind on Galaxy Watches; like with all the best smartwatches, saving space on such a small screen is key to making a solid wearable. While an orange or red dot can be found on the far left of your watch face, other symbols can appear at the top and bottom of the watch. At the top, you might see a phone icon with a slash through it (meaning your watch has lost its Bluetooth connection with your phone), a rectangle with a cloud in the middle (indicating that your watch is connected to your phone with mobile data or Wi-Fi instead of Bluetooth), or a padlock (which means the watch is locked and you'll need your password or PIN to open it).
At the bottom, a blue music note may appear, which tells you whether any app is playing music, as well as if that music is paused — and you can tap the icon to control that audio. Alternatively, a green phone icon could show up in that same spot. This appears when the watch or a connected phone is being used for a call.

title_en: Why you should never point a laser pointer at a security camera
title_fa: Why you should never point a laser pointer at a security camera
excerpt_en: Laser pointers are known to damage security cameras, but do they really? Here's what damage can actually be done.
excerpt_fa: Laser pointers are known to damage security cameras, but do they really? Here's what damage can actually be done.
content_en:
Why you should never point a laser pointer at a security camera
The amount of damage it could do depends on your laser. And your camera.
Opening a door with a hairpin is a common cliché in books, movies and video games. If you are a fan of Better Call Saul, you might have seen a different way of escaping a more technologically advanced capture. In the episode called "Wiedersehen" (Season Four Episode Nine), Werner Ziegler uses a laser pointer to blind a security camera. His escape is only discovered when Mike Ehrmantraut notices some dead pixels on the monitor feeds and finds the pointer. Only it was too late, and Ziegler had already escaped. The trick is clever — but does this work in real life? Well, kind of.
Laser pointers can blind security cameras. In some cases, they can even damage them permanently. However, this would require a combination of three things: a very powerful laser, an older camera and an extremely steady pulse. Possible, but difficult. In most places, it is also illegal. In 2021, a Clearwater man got arrested for pointing a laser at several surveillance cameras owned by the Church of Scientology. The laser did not destroy the cameras, but it did leave dead spots on their lenses, resulting in over $2,000 in damages. Still, the cameras were able to catch him red-handed.
What effect does a laser have on a security camera?
Lasers emit concentrated beams of light at a high intensity. Cameras, meanwhile, are built to convert light into electrical charges, which are then processed and turned into digital video frames. For this reason, security cameras are more susceptible to strong lights than the human eye. Often, exposure to intense light sources such as bright headlights or sunlight reflections can cause the lens to be overwhelmed with light, leading to glare or temporary whiteout effects in footage. Laser pointers can create a similar effect, but stronger.
Most CCTV cameras use either complementary metal-oxide semiconductor (CMOS) or charge-coupled device (CCD) sensors, which can be targeted directly by laser pointers for a sustained period of time. The laser would overwhelm the camera sensor, temporarily blinding it. Moreover, high-intensity lasers also produce heat. Prolonged exposure to this would result in dead pixels and dark spots in the resulting image. In the worst cases, larger "dead areas" would leave the camera unusable.
Modern cameras are more laser-resistant
Not all lasers can actually damage a camera. It would only be possible with a high-powered laser held still for about 10 seconds. If a laser has an output power under 5mW, it is unlikely to cause anything more than a temporary glare on the camera. The problem? Under US Food and Drug Administration regulations, handheld laser pointers that exceed 5mW of output power are illegal to market, sell or promote. For this reason, anyone with a laser that could actually damage a camera is likely to face larger problems than the damage done to the lens.
Let's say that someone had access to a high-powered laser and pointed it directly at a security camera. Even then, it would be difficult for them to cause real long-term damage. As it turns out, it is not easy to hold one's hand steady and aim straight at a camera lens from a distance for a long time. When researchers at IPVM tried using a laser to blind a security camera, they found it "very difficult" to keep the laser focused on an object from roughly 5 feet away "without their hands shaking off target." At this distance, the team could not cause any permanent damage to the security cameras, regardless of the strength of the laser used.
Even with a high-powered laser and good aim, damaging a modern camera would still be difficult, due to newer technology and sensor protections. Vince Gilligan, co-creator of Better Call Saul, even admitted on a podcast that Ziegler's trick would only work on a camera model from the 1960s.
How to prevent (and address) laser damage in your camera
It is impossible to make a standard home security camera completely laser-proof. However, there are preventative measures that can be taken to protect security cameras and make damaging them more difficult. The key is access.
To laser-proof a camera, the simplest solution is to keep it somewhere high or at an angle. This would make it difficult for anyone to aim at it for a prolonged period, as the IPVM team found. Moving security cameras are also harder to aim at. Additionally, using several cameras to cover the same area increases protection. Overlapping coverage would ensure that there are no blind spots, even if one of the cameras is damaged. Finally, many modern cameras allow the installation of security systems that can detect sudden changes in light or unusual activity. This way, if a camera view is blocked or hit with a bright beam, the system can send an instant phone alert.

title_en: How to use Google's SynthID AI detection website
title_fa: How to use Google's SynthID AI detection website
excerpt_en: It's a simple way to check whether an image has been created or manipulated, with a few caveats.
excerpt_fa: It's a simple way to check whether an image has been created or manipulated, with a few caveats.
content_en:
How to use Google's SynthID AI detection website
It's a simple way to check whether an image has been created or manipulated, with a few caveats.
With the proliferation of generative AI tools pumping out images, videos and even songs in recent years, it's hard to spend time on the internet without wondering whether what you're seeing or hearing is real. Google, itself one of the largest purveyors of generative AI, is now making it easier to spot its output. With the new SynthID Detector, anyone can check an image, video, or audio file to see if it's been AI generated, with some major caveats.
Google introduced SynthID in 2023, which adds an imperceptible label to AI-generated content, but there was no way for regular users to actually check for one until now. In 2025, it launched a limited version of SynthID Detector for certain researchers and journalists, and now it's available for everyone. While that may be good news for anyone looking for a way to verify whether a piece of content was generated with AI, it's far from foolproof.
How SynthID Detector works
Since the launch of SynthID, Google's Gemini AI model has embedded a watermark in everything it creates. SynthID Detector works by scanning for that watermark and giving users a simple yes or no answer as to whether one was found. To use the newly available tool, you just need to go to SynthID.com, upload an image, video or audio file, and wait a few seconds for Google to return a result.
That's a big improvement over Google's previous process. Before now, users could ask Gemini itself if a piece of content was AI generated. But for anyone who doesn't trust generative AI, it's hard to take Gemini at its word, and it's an immediate no-go for people who are trying to avoid the technology altogether. SynthID Detector also allows users to scan for watermarks embedded in content created by Google's SynthID partners, which wasn't possible before. That means the new tool can tell whether media was made with AI models from OpenAI, NVIDIA and Kakao, in addition to Gemini. Apple also participates in SynthID, but support for the detector to identify its creations is still in the works.
How reliable is SynthID Detector?
Since SynthID Detector is simply checking for a watermark rather than analyzing media for patterns that indicate AI use, it should eliminate the chance of false positives. That simplicity introduces its own limitations, though. The most obvious one is that it can't detect media made with AI models that don't use SynthID, such as Meta's tools. SynthID Detector is also limited to telling users whether it finds a label in an uploaded file, without providing any information on what parts of it were AI-generated.
Google says its SynthID signatures persist even if AI generations are edited after being created. While there's no guarantee that an enterprising faker won't find a way around that eventually, the company does seem to be taking steps to avoid that. A Google spokesperson reportedly told Ars Technica that users are limited to around 10 checks per day in order to prevent them from using the detector's output to find a way to remove SynthID. Users also have to be logged in to either a Google, OpenAI, or Apple account to use SynthID Detector.
How does SynthID Detector compare to other AI detectors?
SynthID Detector isn't the only generative AI detector available, but despite its limitations, it's likely one of the most reliable. SynthID partner OpenAI runs its own detector tool, which can pick out AI-confirming metadata as well as SynthID watermarks. Meta embeds its own watermark, called Content Seal, into its AI creations and offers a web-based detector tool, though a 2026 report from Reuters found that it sometimes failed to accurately spot them. Companies like Anthropic and Microsoft have also begun watermarking AI media, but don't currently offer consumer tools to detect them.
The downside of all of these tools is that they're designed to detect a specific AI marker, and no reliable detector exists that can spot generative AI across the board. Many researchers have developed their own AI-spotting tools, but they're not available to the public. And when it comes to the general purpose AI detectors that are openly available, their results are unreliable and prone to flag human-created work as AI content.

title_en: An Xbox Series X can now run PlayStation 5 games, but there's a catch
title_fa: An Xbox Series X can now run PlayStation 5 games, but there's a catch
excerpt_en: The idea of PS5 games running on an Xbox Series X -- made possible by how both consoles were built around closely matched hardware -- is certainly exciting.
excerpt_fa: The idea of PS5 games running on an Xbox Series X -- made possible by how both consoles were built around closely matched hardware -- is certainly exciting.
content_en:
An Xbox Series X can now run PlayStation 5 games, but there’s a catch
What is the PS5X Emulator for Xbox Series X and how does it work?
In a YouTube video that went live on September 8, developer Devran Cosmo Uenal booted the PlayStation 5 version of Quake II on an Xbox Series X and played it with an Xbox controller. But the game was running through PS5X, Uenal's Xbox port of the open-source PS5 emulator KytyPS5, and he has gotten three more PS5 games working alongside it.
The fact that he's managed to get PS5 games running on an Xbox at all is super cool, but there's a catch: PS5X only works in the console's official Developer Mode, where Microsoft's documentation caps games at 5GB of memory. That unfortunately rules out the majority of current-gen games, and there's no public download for anyone else to try yet.
How PS5X works
Sony and Microsoft built their current consoles around closely matched AMD hardware. Both of them have eight Zen 2 CPU cores, RDNA 2 graphics and 16GB of GDDR6 memory, and PS5 games are compiled for the same x86-64 processor architecture that PCs use. That means the KytyPS5 emulator can run their code on the host CPU instead of recreating the PS5's hardware in software. Its developer calls it a compatibility layer and, practically, it behaves more like a translator, converting what a PS5 game asks for into something a PC can understand.
KytyPS5 translates the PS5's graphics commands and recompiles its shaders for Vulkan. As a result, it needs a Vulkan 1.3 graphics card on PC, but Xbox Developer Mode only supports DirectX 11 and DirectX 12. "Since Vulkan isn't supported, everything needs to be translated to DirectX," Uenal wrote in the YouTube video's description, where he also admitted that AI was involved in the work. As VideoCardz pointed out, that means fixes the KytyPS5 team makes to its PC renderer have to be adapted before PS5X can use them.
Uenal's video also describes PS5X as a "research project" for "running PS5 homebrew and game backups" on a Series X in Developer Mode. He claims that it doesn't include any PS5 firmware or decryption keys, and KytyPS5's documentation tells users to stick to game files they've obtained legally. Dodging copy protection is ultimately what killed the Switch emulator Yuzu, whose makers settled a Nintendo lawsuit back in 2024 by paying $2.4 million and shutting the project down. The team behind the PS3 emulator RPCS3 lists KytyPS5 and SharpEmu as the two active open-source PS5 emulators that can boot games, and warns players about scam sites posing as real ones.
What PS5X can run
At the time of writing, PS5X runs the PS5 versions of GEX Trilogy, Hellboy: Web of Wyrd, Marvel Cosmic Invasion and Quake II, and all four are compatible with Xbox controller inputs. Some of them have working sound, and TweakTown reckons that Quake II runs at roughly 25 to 45 frames per second in Uenal's footage. It's worth noting that these four games are also sold on other platforms, so there's no sign yet of PS5X running a PS5 exclusive, and Uenal admits that it's early days and that compatibility is limited.

How PS5X works
Sony and Microsoft built their current consoles around closely matched AMD hardware. That means the KytyPS5 emulator can run their code on the host CPU instead of recreating the PS5's hardware in software. Its developer calls it a compatibility layer and, practically, it behaves more like a translator, converting what a PS5 game asks for into something a PC can understand.

title_en: Starlink has two $55 plans that are wildly different — here's how
title_fa: Starlink has two $55 plans that are wildly different — here's how
excerpt_en: It's a trade-off between download speeds and data caps.
excerpt_fa: It's a trade-off between download speeds and data caps.
content_en:
Starlink has two $55 plans that are wildly different — here's how
It's a trade-off between download speeds and data caps.
SpaceX's Starlink has gone through a number of changes over the years when it comes to the different types of satellite-powered internet plans you can subscribe to. But nowadays, the company has settled on a more streamlined offering with its Residential and Roam plans, both of which start at $55 per month.
If you already own a Starlink dish or are willing to rent one through the company itself, you may be wondering which plan you should go with. Despite costing the same amount, the entry-level Residential and Roam tiers aren't interchangeable and choosing one or the other heavily depends on your living situation and what you need the internet for.
We'll breakdown what comes with each tier and the type of people they're best suited for. Note that we're just covering Starlink's Personal plans for individuals and families; the Business plans offer completely different services.
Comparing Residential and Roam
As the name implies, the Residential plan is for those who could use the service in their homes, or at least a fixed location where they're living long-term. All the Residential tiers come with unlimited data, and the big difference between them is how fast your internet speed is.
The basic $55 tier gives you 100 Mbps, which roughly translates to 12.5 megabytes per second for downloading (you can divide your internet speed by eight to get an idea of download times). That's good enough for a small household to browse, stream movies and play games online.
The other two tiers in Residential increase your speed — 200 Mbps for $85 a month, or up to 400 Mbps in Max for $130 — and both get you free professional home installation as well.
Starlink describes the Roam plan as "best for RVs, nomads, and campers, and working on the go," including international travelers. This is the one to choose if you have or plan to own a Starlink Mini dish that you can easily pack in a bag. Unlike the speed-based model in the Residential plans, the basic tiers in Roam give you hard data caps with high-speed internet.
For the $55 tier, you get 100GB per month with speeds of up to 300 Mbps. Once you hit that cap, your connection significantly slows down — just enough for some basic browsing and emailing until your plan renews again. The remaining tiers offer a higher data cap (300GB for $80 a month) and the Unlimited option that removes the cap altogether for $175 a month.
One thing to keep in mind with both Residential and Roam is that you may not always get the advertised speeds on a consistent basis. Starlink's fair use policy states it may temporarily reduce speeds during times of high congestion or peak usage hours in your area.
Before you choose a plan, you can check Starlink's coverage map to see what type of download speeds are available in your state or country. Both types of plans also come with a 30-day trial that allows you to get a full refund within the first month if you aren't satisfied with the internet service.
